extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and students interested in scientific misconduct and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia case-study article documenting the Jan Hendrik Schön scientific misconduct scandal, including allegations, the Bell Labs investigation methods and findings, journal retractions, institutional sanctions, and aftermath. Useful as an example of standards, failures, and responses in research integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of peer review in detecting fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review, traditionally designed to find errors and determine relevance and originality of articles, should also be required to detect deliberate fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scandal 'provoked discussion in the scientific community about the degree of responsibility which coauthors and reviewers of scientific articles bear in cases of scientific misbehavior' and 'mainly concerned whether peer review ... should also be required to detect deliberate fraud.' Use this as a criterion to evaluate expectations placed on peer review vs. other safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent groups must be able to reproduce experimental results; inability to reproduce is a red flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that 'no research group anywhere in the world succeeded in reproducing the results claimed by Schön' and multiple groups tried to reproduce his spectacular claims without success. Extraordinary claims (e.g., new superconductivity, molecular-scale transistors) require independent replication before being accepted as valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raw data retention and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must retain raw data files and laboratory notebooks and provide them when requested during review or investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bell Labs committee 'requested copies of the raw data, but found that Schön had kept no laboratory notebooks. His raw data files had been erased from his computer.' Lack of retained raw data prevents verification and is a serious procedural failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of experimental samples and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental samples, working and non-working devices should be preserved to allow independent examination and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee found 'all of his experimental samples, working, and non-working devices had either been discarded or damaged beyond repair, so the committee was unable to conduct examinations of those.' Preservation supports investigation and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coauthor responsibility and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Coauthors are expected to be sufficiently critical, to validate results, and—where appropriate—to witness or verify key measurements and data handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee found that 'none of the three authors ever saw Schön take measurements from his devices' and while coauthors were exonerated of misconduct, the report criticized whether coauthors were 'sufficiently critical in questioning and validating the results.' This frames a standard for coauthor due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on data fabrication and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Data must be honestly reported; whole data sets must not be reused across different experiments and graphs must be plotted from actual experimental data rather than fabricated mathematical functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report 'found that whole data sets had been reused for a number of different experiments' and that 'some of his graphs ... had instead been produced using mathematical functions.' These practices constitute fabrication/falsification and violate integrity standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation procedures for alleged misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should gather information from coauthors, interview principal contributors, examine drafts and processed numeric data, request raw data, and attempt to inspect physical samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bell Labs committee 'obtained information from all of Schön's coauthors and interviewed the three principal ones,' 'examined electronic drafts of the disputed articles, which included processed numeric data,' requested raw data, and tried to examine samples. These steps describe a model investigation workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reporting and transparency of findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation committees or institutions should publicly report findings and the basis for conclusions about misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bell Labs committee 'released its report publicly' detailing 24 allegations and the evidence found. Public reporting informs the community and supports corrective actions (e.g., retractions, sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional sanctions and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct is substantiated, institutions may impose sanctions such as revoking degrees, banning from funding/committee roles, withdrawing rights to peer review, and other penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the University of Konstanz revoked Schön's doctoral degree; the DFG deprived him of certain rights for eight years; and he faced job consequences. Use these as expected consequences for proven misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' duty to correct the literature (retractions and errata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific journals are responsible for withdrawing or correcting published papers when evidence of fabrication or serious error emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple journals (Science, Nature, Physical Review, Applied Physics Letters, Advanced Materials, etc.) withdrew or retracted many of Schön's articles and published errata/retraction notices. Timely retraction/erratum maintains the integrity of the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-scrutiny detection methods (duplicate values / identical noise patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful scrutiny of published figures and data (looking for duplicated numbers, identical noise patterns across different experiments) can reveal signs of fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scandal began when Julia Hsu and Lynn Loo noticed duplicated numbers and Lydia Sohn observed 'identical noise' in experiments carried out at very different temperatures; Paul McEuen found similar patterns. These are concrete forensic signs to check for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of electronic drafts and processed numeric files for provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic drafts and processed numeric data can provide clues to data processing, reuse, or fabrication and are important evidence during review or investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee 'examined electronic drafts of the disputed articles, which included processed numeric data,' and used them as part of the evidence. Good provenance and documented processing steps aid verification; conversely, absence or suspicious edits are warning signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest and complete reporting of data (including omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must report data honestly and fully; deliberate omission of data to make results appear more convincing is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schön 'acknowledged that the data were incorrect' and claimed some substitutions 'could have occurred by honest mistake' or that he 'omitted some data ... to show more convincing evidence.' Omitting or altering data to misrepresent results violates ethical standards.
